Semiparametric Inference in Panel Data with Interactive
and High-dimensional Confounding

We thank Xun Lu, Anna Mikusheva, Whitney Newey, Zhentao Shi, Liangjun Su, and seminar participants at the CUHK workshop, the 9th International Conference on Econometrics and Statistics, and the 41st Canadian Econometrics Study Group for their useful comments and discussions. Any remaining errors are solely ours.
Bin Chen ††thanks: University of Rochester. Email: binchen@rochester.edu    Yukun Ma ††thanks: University of Rochester. Email: yma69@ur.rochester.edu    Qiyang Yu ††thanks: University of Rochester. Email: qyu13@ur.rochester.edu
November 10, 2026
Abstract

This paper develops inference for a low-dimensional treatment coefficient in partially linear panel models with high-dimensional observed covariates and latent interactive confounding. Flexible adjustment for observed covariates can leave correlated factor components in treatment and outcome residuals, invalidating standard double/debiased machine learning (DML). We propose Factor-Augmented DML (FA-DML), which estimates treatment-side and reduced-form factor spaces from first-stage residuals. The estimator combines a feasible double projection with three-fold, unit-level cross-fitting. The double projection controls interactions between the two estimated factor spaces. The separate folds eliminate same-training-unit pairings in the leading disturbance components of the factor-estimation errors. Under fixed factor ranks, pervasive factor signals, strict exogeneity, and joint asymptotics in the number of units NN and periods TT, FA-DML is first-order equivalent to an infeasible oracle, is asymptotically normal, and admits consistent variance estimation. In the baseline simulation design with strong interactive confounding, FA-DML confidence intervals have coverage close to the nominal level. Standard DML and a two-fold variant that estimates both factor spaces on the same units substantially undercover. In an application to U.S. states, FA-DML finds that a 10%10\% increase in the real minimum wage is associated with a roughly 1.1%1.1\% lower 50/10 wage ratio. The estimate is stable across control sets and first-stage learners.

JEL Codes: C10, C14, C23, C55

Keywords: Debiased machine learning; High-dimensional panel data; Interactive fixed effects; Latent factor confounding; Semiparametric inference.

1 Introduction

Many panel applications have rich observed covariates, yet time-varying unobserved heterogeneity remains a concern. This paper asks how to conduct inference on a low-dimensional treatment coefficient in a partially linear panel model with both observed and latent interactive confounding. In this setting, flexibly residualizing the treatment and outcome with respect to observed covariates does not suffice. The resulting residuals may still contain correlated interactive components generated by common shocks with unit-specific loadings. The usual double/debiased machine learning (DML) score is then contaminated by latent confounding. Additive fixed-effects transformations do not remove these components, while classical interactive fixed-effects (IFE) methods typically impose a parametric specification on the observed part of the model.

DML uses Neyman-orthogonal scores and cross-fitting to make inference robust to regularized or nonparametric first-stage estimation (Chernozhukov et al.,, 2018). Existing panel extensions cover difference-in-differences designs (Chang,, 2020) and partially linear models with additive individual effects (Clarke and Polselli,, 2026). A complementary factor-lasso literature extracts factors from a large set of observed controls and combines them with sparse regression (Hansen and Liao,, 2019). These approaches do not directly address the residual interactive confounding considered here.

High-dimensional common-correlated-effects methods provide a closer comparison. Rücker et al., (2025) construct a factor projection from cross-sectional covariate averages for desparsified Lasso inference, while Chen et al., (2026) combine this projection with DML and unit-level cross-fitting. Both require covariate averages to retain the relevant factor directions, a condition that can fail when factors are absent from the covariates or their loadings cancel across units. The structural projection approach of Dong et al., (2026) uses a related projection idea. It constructs internal instruments by projecting regressors away from a restricted nuisance-function space containing the conditional mean of the structural error. In our setting, the projected spaces are latent and must be estimated.

We propose Factor-Augmented DML (FA-DML). The estimator applies principal component analysis (PCA) to first-stage residuals to estimate the treatment and reduced-form factor spaces, then incorporates both estimated spaces into a double-projection score. It uses three disjoint folds of complete unit histories: one estimates the treatment nuisance function and factor space, a second estimates their reduced-form counterparts, and a third evaluates the score. Coefficient estimates are averaged over the six assignments of fold roles.

This paper makes three contributions. First, it extends DML to partially linear panels with interactive confounding and flexible nuisance functions. The framework allows distinct treatment and outcome factor structures. We establish identification through a factor-orthogonal moment that removes the latent interactive components and is Neyman-orthogonal with respect to the nuisance functions. Under the maintained model, identification follows from strict exogeneity and a projected treatment-variation condition. It does not require the observed covariates to contain signals about the latent factors.

Second, it develops a score and sample-splitting construction that jointly control the additional errors introduced by residual-based factor estimation. Double projection makes the factor–factor remainder a product of treatment-side and reduced-form factor-estimation errors. A single estimated reduced-form projection can instead leave a first-order component or a quadratic self-product with nonzero mean. Estimating the two spaces on separate training folds removes same-unit disturbance pairings from their leading error components, while the evaluation fold separates both estimates from the final moment.

Third, under suitable regularity conditions, we establish oracle-equivalent inference with flexible first-stage learners. The feasible estimator has the same first-order asymptotic distribution as an infeasible estimator that knows the nuisance functions and factor spaces. We derive centered N​T\sqrt{NT}-asymptotic normality and establish consistency of the proposed variance estimator as N,T→∞N,T\to\infty. We also develop an iterative nuclear-norm procedure for selecting the treatment and reduced-form factor dimensions. We prove its consistency and show that estimating these dimensions preserves the inference results.

The simulations separately assess factor augmentation, three-fold separation, regularized nuisance estimation, and rank selection. In the baseline simulations with strong interactive confounding, FA-DML delivers coverage close to the nominal level across linear and nonlinear nuisance specifications and across Lasso and Elastic Net first stages. Standard DML and a two-fold double-projection variant substantially undercover. The proposed rank selector also recovers each factor dimension with high probability in the reported designs.

Our main application studies minimum wages and lower-tail wage inequality in a panel of 5050 U.S. states from 19791979 to 20122012. With factor dimensions chosen by our selector, FA-DML implies that a 10%10\% increase in the real minimum wage is associated with a roughly 1.1%1.1\% lower 50/10 wage ratio. The estimate is stable across Lasso and random-forest first stages and across two control sets. The corresponding 95%95\% confidence intervals exclude zero. With the original controls, pooled OLS, two-way fixed effects, and standard DML yield estimates close to zero, with confidence intervals that include zero. An additional application to branching deregulation is presented in Appendix F.2.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and identification. Section 3 develops the estimator, and Section 4 presents the asymptotic theory and rank-selection results. Section 5 reports the simulations. Section 6 presents the minimum-wage application, and Section 7 concludes. The appendix contains proofs, implementation details, an additional empirical application, and sensitivity analyses.

2 Model and Identification

This section presents the model and a population moment that identifies the target coefficient. Residualizing the outcome and treatment with respect to observed covariates may leave interactive components generated by common shocks and unit-specific loadings. The usual partially linear DML moment can therefore fail. Under the exogeneity and treatment-variation conditions stated below, projecting out the relevant factor spaces yields a valid identifying moment.

2.1 Model and Target Parameter

We observe a balanced panel

{(Yi​t,Di​t,Xi​t):i=1,…,N,t=1,…,T},\{(Y_{it},D_{it},X_{it}):i=1,\ldots,N,\ t=1,\ldots,T\},

where ii indexes units, tt indexes periods, and NN and TT are the corresponding panel dimensions. The variable Yi​tY_{it} is the outcome, Di​tD_{it} is a scalar treatment, and Xi​t∈𝒳X_{it}\in\mathcal{X} is a possibly high-dimensional vector of observed covariates with support 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Let

Yi=(Yi​1,…,Yi​T)′,Di=(Di​1,…,Di​T)′,Xi=(Xi​1,…,Xi​T)′.Y_{i}=(Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{iT})^{\prime},\qquad D_{i}=(D_{i1},\ldots,D_{iT})^{\prime},\qquad X_{i}=(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{iT})^{\prime}.

The unknown functions f0,g0:𝒳→ℝf_{0},g_{0}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} capture how the observed covariates enter the outcome and treatment equations. We use f0​(Xi)f_{0}(X_{i}) and g0​(Xi)g_{0}(X_{i}) for the TT-vectors obtained by evaluating these functions period by period. The parameter of interest is the common coefficient θ0\theta_{0}. Let rY∗r_{Y}^{*} and rDr_{D} denote the outcome-side and treatment-side factor dimensions, respectively. Let GY0∈ℝT×rY∗G_{Y}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times r_{Y}^{*}} and GD0∈ℝT×rDG_{D}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times r_{D}} be full-column-rank matrices of outcome-side and treatment-side common factors, respectively, and let CY,i∗∈ℝrY∗C_{Y,i}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{Y}^{*}} and CD,i∈ℝrDC_{D,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{D}} be their unit-specific loadings. Let εi,νi∈ℝT\varepsilon_{i},\nu_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{T} denote the corresponding idiosyncratic disturbances. The primitive loading arrays are treated as fixed throughout. We consider the partially linear panel system

Yi\displaystyle Y_{i} =Di​θ0+f0​(Xi)+GY0​CY,i∗+εi,\displaystyle=D_{i}\theta_{0}+f_{0}(X_{i})+G_{Y}^{0}C_{Y,i}^{*}+\varepsilon_{i}, (1)
Di\displaystyle D_{i} =g0​(Xi)+GD0​CD,i+νi.\displaystyle=g_{0}(X_{i})+G_{D}^{0}C_{D,i}+\nu_{i}. (2)

Row tt of each factor matrix contains the common-factor values in period tt, while heterogeneity across units enters through the corresponding loadings.11 1 Equation (2) allows common forces to affect treatment differently across units even after adjustment for observed covariates. For example, states may respond differently to national political developments or aggregate economic conditions. These forces may also affect outcomes, generating latent confounding. The additive factor structure is a maintained assumption on treatment assignment. For binary treatment, with fixed loadings, the conditional mean restriction below implies Pr⁡(Di​t=1∣Xi,ℱT)=g0​(Xi​t)+(GD0​CD,i)t∈[0,1].\Pr(D_{it}=1\mid X_{i},\mathcal{F}_{T})=g_{0}(X_{it})+(G_{D}^{0}C_{D,i})_{t}\in[0,1]. A causal interpretation of θ0\theta_{0} requires the outcome equation to be structural and the strict-exogeneity condition stated below to hold.

This rank condition allows dependence between the two sets of loadings but rules out exact linear dependence among their joint columns. The two equations may still share common factors.

GY0​CY,i∗+θ0​GD0​CD,i,i=1,…,N,G_{Y}^{0}C_{Y,i}^{*}+\theta_{0}G_{D}^{0}C_{D,i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,

At θ0=0\theta_{0}=0, the latter equals the structural outcome factor space, so this nesting need not hold. The results are established for each fixed θ0\theta_{0}.

2.2 Why Covariate Residualization Is Not Enough

To see why standard DML fails, first suppose that the observed nuisance functions were known. Define the covariate-residualized treatment and outcome by

vD,i=Di−g0​(Xi),vY,i=Yi−m0​(Xi),v_{D,i}=D_{i}-g_{0}(X_{i}),\qquad v_{Y,i}=Y_{i}-m_{0}(X_{i}),

and define the residual in the outcome equation at the true coefficient by

ui=vY,i−θ0​vD,i.u_{i}=v_{Y,i}-\theta_{0}v_{D,i}.

Equations (1)–(4) imply

vD,i=GD0​CD,i+νi,ui=GY0​CY,i∗+εi.v_{D,i}=G_{D}^{0}C_{D,i}+\nu_{i},\qquad u_{i}=G_{Y}^{0}C_{Y,i}^{*}+\varepsilon_{i}. (6)

The usual partially linear score uses vD,i′​uiv_{D,i}^{\prime}u_{i} (Chernozhukov et al.,, 2018). Even if every term involving νi\nu_{i} or εi\varepsilon_{i} has conditional mean zero given the common factors, this score contains the factor–factor term

CD,i′GD0′GY0CY,i∗.C_{D,i}^{\prime}G_{D}^{0\prime}G_{Y}^{0}C_{Y,i}^{*}.

This term is the inner product of the treatment- and outcome-side factor components. When those components are not orthogonal, the score need not have mean zero. Flexible regression of YiY_{i} and DiD_{i} on XiX_{i} does not solve this problem because the two latent components in (6) remain.

2.4 Two Layers of Orthogonalization

The factor projection addresses latent confounding. A second form of orthogonalization protects the score from first-stage estimation error in the observed nuisance functions. The feasible algorithm estimates factor-residualized versions of these functions. Define

g0∗​(Xi)=MGD0​g0​(Xi),m0∗​(Xi)=MG0​m0​(Xi).g_{0}^{*}(X_{i})=M_{G_{D}^{0}}g_{0}(X_{i}),\qquad m_{0}^{*}(X_{i})=M_{G^{0}}m_{0}(X_{i}).

Although g0g_{0} and m0m_{0} act period by period, the projected functions generally depend on the complete covariate path because the projections mix periods. Under Assumption 1, they generate the same conditional population moment as the unprojected nuisance functions: for every candidate coefficient θ\theta,

E⁡[ψ⁡(Wi,θ,g0,m0,A0)∣ℱT]=E⁡[ψ⁡(Wi,θ,g0∗,m0∗,A0)∣ℱT].E[\psi(W_{i};\theta,g_{0},m_{0},A_{0})\mid\mathcal{F}_{T}]=E[\psi(W_{i};\theta,g_{0}^{*},m_{0}^{*},A_{0})\mid\mathcal{F}_{T}]. (11)

At the true coefficient, the scores also coincide exactly:

ψ⁡(Wi,θ0,g0,m0,A0)=ψ⁡(Wi,θ0,g0∗,m0∗,A0).\psi(W_{i};\theta_{0},g_{0},m_{0},A_{0})=\psi(W_{i};\theta_{0},g_{0}^{*},m_{0}^{*},A_{0}).

Appendix C gives the underlying algebra.

We state the orthogonality property for the projected nuisance functions. Let hg,hm:𝒳T→ℝTh_{g},h_{m}:\mathcal{X}^{T}\to\mathbb{R}^{T} be square-integrable perturbation directions, which may depend on ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}. Under Assumption 1,

∂∂τ​E​[ψ⁡(Wi,θ0,g0∗+τ​hg,m0∗+τ​hm,A0)∣ℱT]|τ=0=0.\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}E\!\left[\psi(W_{i};\theta_{0},g_{0}^{*}+\tau h_{g},m_{0}^{*}+\tau h_{m},A_{0})\mid\mathcal{F}_{T}\right]\right|_{\tau=0}=0. (12)

Thus first-stage errors around g0∗g_{0}^{*} and m0∗m_{0}^{*} have no first-order effect on the population moment. This Neyman orthogonality is distinct from factor orthogonality: the former controls local first-stage error, whereas the latter uses A0A_{0} to remove the latent components themselves. Equality of the conditional population moments preserves the identifying equation, while exact equality at θ0\theta_{0} preserves the oracle score used in the asymptotic expansion. This allows the feasible procedure to target the projected nuisance functions.

3 Estimation

This section develops the feasible FA-DML estimator. The population-moment equivalence and the exact score identity at θ0\theta_{0} established in Section 2 permit the algorithm to target the projected nuisance functions g0∗g_{0}^{*} and m0∗m_{0}^{*}, together with the latent factor spaces span⁡(GD0)\operatorname{span}(G_{D}^{0}) and span⁡(G0)\operatorname{span}(G^{0}). The estimator uses machine-learning (ML) estimates of the nuisance functions and PCA estimates of the factor spaces. Three-fold cross-fitting separates treatment-side training, reduced-form training, and score evaluation.

For the analysis below, define the augmented loadings

C¯D,i=CD,i+(GD0′GD0)−1GD0′g0(Xi),C¯Y,i=Ci+(G0′G0)−1G0′m0(Xi),\bar{C}_{D,i}=C_{D,i}+(G_{D}^{0\prime}G_{D}^{0})^{-1}G_{D}^{0\prime}g_{0}(X_{i}),\qquad\bar{C}_{Y,i}=C_{i}+(G^{0\prime}G^{0})^{-1}G^{0\prime}m_{0}(X_{i}),

and let ξi=θ0​νi+εi\xi_{i}=\theta_{0}\nu_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}. The projected residuals then satisfy

vD,i∗=Di−g0∗​(Xi)=GD0​C¯D,i+νi,vY,i∗=Yi−m0∗​(Xi)=G0​C¯Y,i+ξi.v_{D,i}^{*}=D_{i}-g_{0}^{*}(X_{i})=G_{D}^{0}\bar{C}_{D,i}+\nu_{i},\qquad v_{Y,i}^{*}=Y_{i}-m_{0}^{*}(X_{i})=G^{0}\bar{C}_{Y,i}+\xi_{i}. (13)

By (5), θ0​GD0​C¯D,i∈span⁡(G0)\theta_{0}G_{D}^{0}\bar{C}_{D,i}\in\operatorname{span}(G^{0}). Hence there is a unique C¯i∈ℝrY\bar{C}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{Y}} satisfying

G0​C¯i=G0​C¯Y,i−θ0​GD0​C¯D,i.G^{0}\bar{C}_{i}=G^{0}\bar{C}_{Y,i}-\theta_{0}G_{D}^{0}\bar{C}_{D,i}.

Thus the projected score residual at θ0\theta_{0} is

ui∗=vY,i∗−θ0​vD,i∗=G0​C¯i+εi.u_{i}^{*}=v_{Y,i}^{*}-\theta_{0}v_{D,i}^{*}=G^{0}\bar{C}_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}. (14)

The augmented loadings C¯D,i\bar{C}_{D,i} and C¯Y,i\bar{C}_{Y,i} determine the factor signal available to PCA, whereas C¯i\bar{C}_{i} enters the score expansion.

3.1 Three-Fold Double-Projection Estimator

The sample is split into three folds of complete unit-level time series. For each split, the treatment-side first stage, the reduced-form first stage, and score evaluation are performed on mutually disjoint folds. Algorithm 1 treats rDr_{D} and rYr_{Y} as given. Section 4.4 establishes validity with estimated ranks, and the complete data-driven rank-selection procedure appears in Algorithm 2 in Appendix B. The algorithm uses the same construction for all coefficient values; it does not require a preliminary test on θ0\theta_{0} or impose an ordering on the two factor dimensions.

Algorithm 1 (Three-fold double-projection estimator).

Given panel data {(Yi,Di,Xi):i=1,…,N}\{(Y_{i},D_{i},X_{i}):i=1,\dots,N\}, factor dimensions rDr_{D} and rYr_{Y}, fold-specific initializations for g^\hat{g} and m^\hat{m}, a maximum number of iterations SS, and a tolerance ϵtol>0\epsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}>0:

  1. 1.

    Partition {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\} into three disjoint folds ℐ1,ℐ2,ℐ3\mathcal{I}_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2},\mathcal{I}_{3}, and let (ℐ1(l),ℐ2(l),ℐ3(l))(\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)},\mathcal{I}_{2}^{(l)},\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}), l=1,…,6l=1,\dots,6, denote their six permutations.

  2. 2.

    For each l=1,…,6l=1,\dots,6, proceed as follows.

    1. (a)

      On ℐ1(l)\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)}, initialize g^\hat{g} using only this fold. Estimate g0∗g_{0}^{*} and span⁡(GD0)\operatorname{span}(G_{D}^{0}) by alternating between two updates: (i) apply rank-rDr_{D} PCA to {Di−g^​(Xi):i∈ℐ1(l)}\{D_{i}-\hat{g}(X_{i}):i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)}\} to obtain G^D\hat{G}_{D}; (ii) refit g^\hat{g} with the chosen first-stage method to the projected responses {MG^D​Di:i∈ℐ1(l)}\{M_{\hat{G}_{D}}D_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)}\}.44 4 Because the projector mixes periods, the learner must map the complete path XiX_{i} to a TT-vector, or use an equivalent stacked design. For linear or series learners, project the stacked design along with the response. A learner using only Xi​tX_{it} at row tt requires the projected target to remain a function of Xi​tX_{it} alone. Stop after SS updates or when the root-mean-square change in fitted values on the fold is at most ϵtol\epsilon_{\mathrm{tol}}. After the final update, apply PCA once more to align the final nuisance and factor estimates; denote them by g^(l​1)\hat{g}^{(l1)} and G^D(l​1)\hat{G}_{D}^{(l1)}.

    2. (b)

      On ℐ2(l)\mathcal{I}_{2}^{(l)}, analogously initialize m^\hat{m} using only this fold and estimate m0∗m_{0}^{*} and span⁡(G0)\operatorname{span}(G^{0}) from the outcome residuals using rank rYr_{Y}. Denote the outputs by m^(l​2)\hat{m}^{(l2)} and G^(l​2)\hat{G}^{(l2)}.

    3. (c)

      On the evaluation fold ℐ3(l)\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}, form the feasible counterparts of vD,i∗v_{D,i}^{*} and vY,i∗v_{Y,i}^{*}:

      v^D,i=Di−g^(l​1)​(Xi),v^Y,i=Yi−m^(l​2)​(Xi),i∈ℐ3(l).\hat{v}_{D,i}=D_{i}-\hat{g}^{(l1)}(X_{i}),\qquad\hat{v}_{Y,i}=Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{(l2)}(X_{i}),\qquad i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}.

      Let A^(l)=MG^D(l​1)​MG^(l​2)\hat{A}^{(l)}=M_{\hat{G}_{D}^{(l1)}}M_{\hat{G}^{(l2)}} and compute

      θ^(l)\displaystyle\hat{\theta}^{(l)} =∑i∈ℐ3(l)v^D,i′​A^(l)​v^Y,i∑i∈ℐ3(l)v^D,i′​A^(l)​v^D,i,\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}^{(l)}\hat{v}_{Y,i}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}^{(l)}\hat{v}_{D,i}},
      J^l\displaystyle\hat{J}_{l} =1T​|ℐ3(l)|​∑i∈ℐ3(l)v^D,i′​A^(l)​v^D,i,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T|\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}^{(l)}\hat{v}_{D,i},
      σ^θ,l2\displaystyle\hat{\sigma}_{\theta,l}^{2} =J^l−2T​|ℐ3(l)|​∑i∈ℐ3(l){v^D,i′​A^(l)​(v^Y,i−θ^(l)​v^D,i)}2.\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{J}_{l}^{-2}}{T|\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\left\{\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}^{(l)}(\hat{v}_{Y,i}-\hat{\theta}^{(l)}\hat{v}_{D,i})\right\}^{2}.

      If ∑i∈ℐ3(l)v^D,i′​A^(l)​v^D,i=0\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}^{(l)}\hat{v}_{D,i}=0, set θ^(l)=σ^θ,l2=0\hat{\theta}^{(l)}=\hat{\sigma}_{\theta,l}^{2}=0 for that split. Proposition 2 shows that this convention is invoked with probability approaching zero.

    Average across the six permutations to symmetrize over fold roles:

    θ^=16​∑l=16θ^(l),σ^θ2=16​∑l=16σ^θ,l2.\hat{\theta}=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{l=1}^{6}\hat{\theta}^{(l)},\qquad\hat{\sigma}_{\theta}^{2}=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{l=1}^{6}\hat{\sigma}_{\theta,l}^{2}.

3.2 Why Double Projection and Three-Fold Cross-Fitting?

Double projection turns the factor–factor remainder into a cross-product of estimation errors from the two factor spaces. Separate training folds remove same-unit disturbance pairings from its leading component, while the evaluation fold separates both estimates from the final score.

Fix one permutation ll, write n3=|ℐ3(l)|n_{3}=|\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}|, and suppress fold superscripts. Let A^=MG^D​MG^\hat{A}=M_{\hat{G}_{D}}M_{\hat{G}}. Consider the factor–factor term in the score expansion:

1n3​T∑i∈ℐ3(l)C¯D,i′GD0′A^G0C¯i.\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{3}T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\bar{C}_{D,i}^{\prime}G_{D}^{0\prime}\hat{A}G^{0}\bar{C}_{i}. (15)

Its oracle counterpart is zero, so this term arises entirely from factor estimation.

Let HDH_{D} and HGH_{G} be the nonsingular rotation matrices and write

ℰD=GD0​HD−G^D,ℰG=G0​HG−G^.\mathcal{E}_{D}=G_{D}^{0}H_{D}-\hat{G}_{D},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{G}=G^{0}H_{G}-\hat{G}.

Since G^D′​A^=0\hat{G}_{D}^{\prime}\hat{A}=0 and A^​G^=0\hat{A}\hat{G}=0,

GD0′A^G0=HD−⁣′ℰD′A^ℰGHG−1.G_{D}^{0\prime}\hat{A}G^{0}=H_{D}^{-\prime}\mathcal{E}_{D}^{\prime}\hat{A}\mathcal{E}_{G}H_{G}^{-1}. (16)

Thus double projection makes the factor–factor term depend on a product of errors from the two estimated spaces, without requiring nesting.

With only the outcome-side projector, the corresponding matrix is

GD0′MG^G0=GD0′MG^ℰGHG−1.G_{D}^{0\prime}M_{\hat{G}}G^{0}=G_{D}^{0\prime}M_{\hat{G}}\mathcal{E}_{G}H_{G}^{-1}.

Without nesting, this expression can retain a first-order component in the reduced-form factor error. Under nesting, it becomes a quadratic self-product of that error, which can contain same-training-unit disturbance terms.

The cross-product in (16) allows these pairings to be removed by separate training folds. Recall that ξi=θ0​νi+εi\xi_{i}=\theta_{0}\nu_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}. Up to the finite-dimensional coefficient matrices in the PCA expansions, the leading disturbance product with the oracle operator is

1n1​n2​∑j∈ℐ1(l)∑k∈ℐ2(l)C¯D,j​C¯Y,k′​νj′​A0​ξk.\frac{1}{n_{1}n_{2}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{2}^{(l)}}\bar{C}_{D,j}\bar{C}_{Y,k}^{\prime}\nu_{j}^{\prime}A_{0}\xi_{k}.

For disjoint training folds, every pair has j≠kj\neq k. Conditional on the factor paths and training covariates, the summands have mean zero by cross-sectional independence and the disturbance mean restrictions.

If both factor spaces were estimated on a common training fold, the product would also contain same-unit terms involving νj′​A0​ξj\nu_{j}^{\prime}A_{0}\xi_{j}. Under the exogeneity conditions,

E⁡[νj′​A0​ξj∣ℱT]=θ0​tr⁡(A0​E​[νj​νj′∣ℱT]),E[\nu_{j}^{\prime}A_{0}\xi_{j}\mid\mathcal{F}_{T}]=\theta_{0}\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A_{0}E[\nu_{j}\nu_{j}^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{F}_{T}]\right),

which need not vanish. Separate training folds exclude these same-unit terms, while the third fold separates both factor estimates from score evaluation.

4 Theory

This section establishes the asymptotic validity of the three-fold double-projection FA-DML estimator introduced in Section 3. We show that the feasible score, which uses estimated nuisance functions and estimated factor spaces, is first-order equivalent to the infeasible oracle score

1N​T​∑i=1Nνi′​A0​εi.\frac{1}{\sqrt{NT}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nu_{i}^{\prime}A_{0}\varepsilon_{i}.

Consequently, the proposed estimator is centered at θ0\theta_{0} and admits standard N​T\sqrt{NT}-inference.

4.1 Oracle Decomposition

Fix one split l∈{1,…,6}l\in\{1,\dots,6\}, write nk=|ℐk(l)|n_{k}=|\mathcal{I}_{k}^{(l)}| for k=1,2,3k=1,2,3, and suppress the superscript ll on fold-specific quantities whenever there is no ambiguity. We retain the population and augmented-loading notation introduced in Sections 2 and 3. Define

δig=g^(l​1)​(Xi)−g0∗​(Xi),δim=m^(l​2)​(Xi)−m0∗​(Xi),\delta_{i}^{g}=\hat{g}^{(l1)}(X_{i})-g_{0}^{*}(X_{i}),\qquad\delta_{i}^{m}=\hat{m}^{(l2)}(X_{i})-m_{0}^{*}(X_{i}),

and write

δi=δim−θ0​δig,ΔA=A^−A0.\delta_{i}=\delta_{i}^{m}-\theta_{0}\delta_{i}^{g},\qquad\Delta_{A}=\hat{A}-A_{0}.

Equations (13) and (14) then give

v^D,i=GD0​C¯D,i+νi−δig,v^Y,i−θ0​v^D,i=G0​C¯i+εi−δi.\hat{v}_{D,i}=G_{D}^{0}\bar{C}_{D,i}+\nu_{i}-\delta_{i}^{g},\qquad\hat{v}_{Y,i}-\theta_{0}\hat{v}_{D,i}=G^{0}\bar{C}_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}-\delta_{i}.

Throughout this section, we maintain the model and joint loading-rank condition in Section 2. The coefficient θ0\theta_{0} is fixed, and all nuisance functions and factor spaces below refer to the corresponding data-generating process (DGP). Until Section 4.4, the ranks rDr_{D} and rYr_{Y} are treated as fixed and known, as formalized in Assumption 4(a). Because their defining projections depend on the factor paths, g0∗g_{0}^{*} and m0∗m_{0}^{*} are ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}-measurable random maps. Unless a statement explicitly conditions on a specified sigma field, all OpO_{p} and opo_{p} orders refer to the joint law of the sample, the factor paths, the random partition, and any auxiliary learner randomization.

The splitwise estimator can be written as

θ^(l)−θ0=∑i∈ℐ3(l)v^D,i′​A^​(v^Y,i−θ0​v^D,i)∑i∈ℐ3(l)v^D,i′​A^​v^D,i.\hat{\theta}^{(l)}-\theta_{0}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}(\hat{v}_{Y,i}-\theta_{0}\hat{v}_{D,i})}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}\hat{v}_{D,i}}. (17)

Expanding the numerator yields

θ^(l)−θ0=(∑i∈ℐ3(l)v^D,i′​A^​v^D,i)−1​(∑i∈ℐ3(l)νi′​A0​εi+∑i∈ℐ3(l)R1​i+∑i∈ℐ3(l)R2​i+∑i∈ℐ3(l)R3​i+∑i∈ℐ3(l)R4​i),\displaystyle\hat{\theta}^{(l)}-\theta_{0}=\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\hat{v}_{D,i}^{\prime}\hat{A}\hat{v}_{D,i}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\nu_{i}^{\prime}A_{0}\varepsilon_{i}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}R_{1i}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}R_{2i}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}R_{3i}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}R_{4i}\right), (18)

where

R1​i\displaystyle R_{1i} =−δig′A0εi−νi′A0δi+δig′A0δi,\displaystyle=-\delta_{i}^{g\prime}A_{0}\varepsilon_{i}-\nu_{i}^{\prime}A_{0}\delta_{i}+\delta_{i}^{g\prime}A_{0}\delta_{i},
R2​i\displaystyle R_{2i} =C¯D,i′GD0′A^G0C¯i+C¯D,i′GD0′A^εi+νi′A^G0C¯i,\displaystyle=\bar{C}_{D,i}^{\prime}G_{D}^{0\prime}\hat{A}G^{0}\bar{C}_{i}+\bar{C}_{D,i}^{\prime}G_{D}^{0\prime}\hat{A}\varepsilon_{i}+\nu_{i}^{\prime}\hat{A}G^{0}\bar{C}_{i},

The first term in (18) is the oracle score. The remainder terms R1​iR_{1i}–R4​iR_{4i} collect, respectively, the nuisance-error terms under the oracle projector, the pure factor-projection terms, the projector-perturbation terms, and the factor–nuisance cross terms. The proof of Theorem 1 shows that all four remainder sums are op​(n3​T)o_{p}(\sqrt{n_{3}T}) under its stated assumptions and the three-fold double-projection construction.

4.2 Regularity Conditions

We state the assumptions in four groups. The first concerns first-stage learning and remainder rates. The second concerns the factor structure and fold design. The third concerns training-fold disturbances and residuals, and the fourth concerns evaluation-fold moments.

Recall that ℱT=σ⁡(GD0,GY0)\mathcal{F}_{T}=\sigma(G_{D}^{0},G_{Y}^{0}) is the sigma field generated by the factor paths. For each split ll, let ℋl\mathcal{H}_{l} be the sigma field generated by ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}, the ordered random partition, any auxiliary learner randomization, and the training data

{(Yi,Di,Xi):i∈ℐ1(l)∪ℐ2(l)}.\{(Y_{i},D_{i},X_{i}):i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)}\cup\mathcal{I}_{2}^{(l)}\}.

Any auxiliary learner randomization is independent of the sample and partition conditional on ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}. The treatment learner g^(l)\hat{g}^{(l)} is trained on ℐ1(l)\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)}, and the reduced-form learner m^(l)\hat{m}^{(l)} is trained on ℐ2(l)\mathcal{I}_{2}^{(l)}. Both are ℋl\mathcal{H}_{l}-measurable.

For any ℋl\mathcal{H}_{l}-measurable map h:𝒳T→ℝTh:\mathcal{X}^{T}\to\mathbb{R}^{T}, define the conditional prediction norm and evaluation-fold empirical norm by

‖h‖P,2\displaystyle\|h\|_{P,2} ={1T​E​[‖h⁡(Xi)‖22∣ℋl]}1/2,i∈ℐ3(l),\displaystyle=\left\{\frac{1}{T}E\!\left[\|h(X_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{l}\right]\right\}^{1/2},\qquad i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)},
‖h‖n,l\displaystyle\|h\|_{n,l} ={1T​n3​∑i∈ℐ3(l)‖h⁡(Xi)‖22}1/2.\displaystyle=\left\{\frac{1}{Tn_{3}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\|h(X_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\right\}^{1/2}.

By Assumption 4(d)–(e), together with the independence of learner randomization, the first expression does not depend on the choice of evaluation unit. We suppress the dependence of the rate sequences on (N,T)(N,T).

Assumption 2 (First-stage prediction rates).

There exist positive deterministic sequences r¯g\bar{r}_{g} and r¯m\bar{r}_{m}, both converging to zero, such that the following conditions hold uniformly over ll.

  1. (a)

    The feasible treatment learner satisfies

    ‖g^(l​1)−g0∗‖P,2=Op​(r¯g).\|\hat{g}^{(l1)}-g_{0}^{*}\|_{P,2}=O_{p}(\bar{r}_{g}).
  2. (b)

    The feasible reduced-form learner satisfies

    ‖m^(l​2)−m0∗‖P,2=Op​(r¯m).\|\hat{m}^{(l2)}-m_{0}^{*}\|_{P,2}=O_{p}(\bar{r}_{m}).
  3. (c)

    The prediction rates satisfy

    n3​T​r¯g​(r¯m+r¯g)=o⁡(1).\sqrt{n_{3}T}\,\bar{r}_{g}\bigl(\bar{r}_{m}+\bar{r}_{g}\bigr)=o(1).

Assumption 2(a)–(b) bounds prediction errors relative to the projected targets g0∗g_{0}^{*} and m0∗m_{0}^{*}. Part (c) makes the quadratic nuisance-error term asymptotically negligible. The proof of Proposition 1 transfers the conditional prediction bounds to the evaluation fold and establishes the resulting bound on R1​iR_{1i}.

There exist positive deterministic sequences ηg\eta_{g} and ηm\eta_{m} such that the following conditions hold uniformly over ll. Write η=(ηg2+ηm2)1/2\eta=(\eta_{g}^{2}+\eta_{m}^{2})^{1/2}.

  1. (a)

    The loading-weighted first-stage errors satisfy

    ‖1n1​T​∑i∈ℐ1(l)δig​C¯D,i′‖F\displaystyle\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{1}T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{1}^{(l)}}\delta_{i}^{g}\bar{C}_{D,i}^{\prime}\right\|_{F} =Op​(ηg),\displaystyle=O_{p}(\eta_{g}), ‖1n2​T​∑i∈ℐ2(l)δim​C¯Y,i′‖F\displaystyle\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{2}T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2}^{(l)}}\delta_{i}^{m}\bar{C}_{Y,i}^{\prime}\right\|_{F} =Op​(ηm),\displaystyle=O_{p}(\eta_{m}),
    ‖1n3​T​∑i∈ℐ3(l)δig​C¯i′‖F\displaystyle\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{3}T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\delta_{i}^{g}\bar{C}_{i}^{\prime}\right\|_{F} =Op​(ηg),\displaystyle=O_{p}(\eta_{g}), ‖1n3​T​∑i∈ℐ3(l)δi​C¯D,i′‖F\displaystyle\left\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{3}T}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\delta_{i}\bar{C}_{D,i}^{\prime}\right\|_{F} =Op​(η).\displaystyle=O_{p}(\eta).

    Let qN​T=T−1/2+T/Nq_{NT}=T^{-1/2}+\sqrt{T}/N. The associated rate sequences also satisfy

    TN​ηg2=o⁡(1),TN​ηm2=o⁡(1),TN​ηg​η=o⁡(1),\frac{T}{N}\eta_{g}^{2}=o(1),\qquad\frac{T}{N}\eta_{m}^{2}=o(1),\qquad\sqrt{\frac{T}{N}}\,\eta_{g}\eta=o(1),

    and

    qN​T​(1+ηg+ηm)=o⁡(1),NT​qN​T2=o⁡(1).q_{NT}(1+\eta_{g}+\eta_{m})=o(1),\qquad\sqrt{\frac{N}{T}}\,q_{NT}^{2}=o(1).
  2. (b)

    The evaluation-fold errors satisfy the loading-weighted squared-error bounds

    1n3​T​∑i∈ℐ3(l)‖δig‖22​‖C¯i‖22\displaystyle\frac{1}{n_{3}T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\|\delta_{i}^{g}\|_{2}^{2}\|\bar{C}_{i}\|_{2}^{2} =Op​(ηg2),\displaystyle=O_{p}(\eta_{g}^{2}), 1n3​T​∑i∈ℐ3(l)‖δi‖22​‖C¯D,i‖22\displaystyle\frac{1}{n_{3}T}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\|\delta_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\|\bar{C}_{D,i}\|_{2}^{2} =Op​(η2),\displaystyle=O_{p}(\eta^{2}),

    and the fourth-moment bound

    1n3​T2​∑i∈ℐ3(l)‖δig‖24=Op​(1).\frac{1}{n_{3}T^{2}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}\|\delta_{i}^{g}\|_{2}^{4}=O_{p}(1).

Assumption 3(a) controls the loading-weighted errors in the PCA expansions and their interactions with the score. The rate restrictions bound the corresponding first-stage terms and quadratic PCA remainders. Part (b), needed only for variance consistency, controls squared errors without uniformly bounding individual loadings. These conditions complement the prediction bounds in Assumption 2. Appendix D discusses their roles and gives a Lasso illustration.

The basis G0G^{0} is chosen measurably with respect to ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}, so the reduced-form coordinates CiC_{i} are ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}-measurable. Cross-sectional sampling statements are conditional on ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}.

Assumption 4 (Factor structure, fold design, and sampling).

The following conditions hold as N,T→∞N,T\to\infty.

  1. (a)

    The factor dimensions rDr_{D} and rYr_{Y} are positive integers that remain fixed.

  2. (b)

    There exist constants 0<c<C<∞0<c<C<\infty such that, with probability approaching one, all eigenvalues of

    1N∑i=1NC¯D,iC¯D,i′,1N∑i=1NC¯Y,iC¯Y,i′,1TGD0′GD0,1TG0′G0\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{C}_{D,i}\bar{C}_{D,i}^{\prime},\quad\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bar{C}_{Y,i}\bar{C}_{Y,i}^{\prime},\quad\frac{1}{T}G_{D}^{0\prime}G_{D}^{0},\quad\frac{1}{T}G^{0\prime}G^{0}

    lie in [c,C][c,C].

  3. (c)

    The augmented loadings satisfy

    1N​∑i=1N(‖C¯D,i‖24+‖C¯Y,i‖24)=Op​(1).\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\|\bar{C}_{D,i}\|_{2}^{4}+\|\bar{C}_{Y,i}\|_{2}^{4}\right)=O_{p}(1).
  4. (d)

    The ordered partition (ℐ1,ℐ2,ℐ3)(\mathcal{I}_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2},\mathcal{I}_{3}) of {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\} is drawn uniformly at random from all such partitions whose fold sizes differ by at most one. It is independent of the full triangular array including the factor paths, primitive loadings, covariates, and errors.

  5. (e)

    Conditional on ℱT\mathcal{F}_{T}, the unit-level arrays {(Xi,εi,νi)}i=1N\{(X_{i},\varepsilon_{i},\nu_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} are independent across ii, and the covariate paths XiX_{i} have a common conditional distribution. The conditional distributions of (εi,νi)(\varepsilon_{i},\nu_{i}) need not be identical across units.

Assumption 4 collects the factor-structure and sample-splitting requirements. Part (b) bounds the eigenvalues of the factor and augmented-loading Gram matrices used by PCA without separately imposing primitive-loading pervasiveness. Part (c) bounds average fourth moments, not the largest loading in the sample.

By the definition of C¯i\bar{C}_{i},

Thus no separate moment restriction on C¯i\bar{C}_{i} is needed. Parts (d)–(e) specify balanced random folds and conditional cross-sectional independence. Assumption 6 imposes high-level conditional-moment conditions on the held-out evaluation fold, conditional on the sigma field 𝒢l\mathcal{G}_{l}, which collects the population factor space, the training-fold information and the evaluation-fold covariates. Part (a) is the score-relevant conditional exogeneity restriction; it does not require conditional independence between νi\nu_{i} and εi\varepsilon_{i}. Part (b) supplies the Lyapunov condition for the conditional central limit theorem (CLT). Part (c) specifies the positive limits of the normalized score variance and the ordered-score denominator, which determine Ω0\Omega_{0} and κ0\kappa_{0}.

Assumption 6 does not cover generic dynamic-panel specifications with predetermined regressors. Extending the FA-DML framework to dynamic panels would require a separate treatment of predetermined regressors, the resulting additional score terms, and the interaction between dynamic endogeneity and factor estimation. We leave this extension for future research.

1T​n3​∑i∈ℐ3(l)R1​i=Op​(r¯g+r¯m+T​n3​r¯g​(r¯m+r¯g))=op​(1).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{Tn_{3}}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{3}^{(l)}}R_{1i}=O_{p}\!\left(\bar{r}_{g}+\bar{r}_{m}+\sqrt{Tn_{3}}\,\bar{r}_{g}\left(\bar{r}_{m}+\bar{r}_{g}\right)\right)=o_{p}(1).

The proof of Proposition 1 shows that the prediction rates carry over to the evaluation fold and make the nuisance-error remainder negligible. The first-stage learners may be chosen flexibly, provided their final feasible estimates satisfy the stated prediction, loading-weighted, and residual conditions.

4.3 Main Inference Results

We first state the asymptotic distribution of the FA-DML estimator when the factor dimensions rDr_{D} and rYr_{Y} are treated as fixed and known. Rank selection is discussed in Section 4.4. Assumption 1 gives the population identification conditions. For the inference results below, exogeneity and asymptotic nondegeneracy are imposed directly through the fold-specific conditions in Assumptions 5 and 6.

Theorem 1 (Asymptotic normality of the estimator).

Suppose Assumption 2, Assumption 3(a), Assumption 4, Assumption 5(a),(b),(d), and Assumption 6 hold. Then

N​T​(θ^−θ0)→𝑑N⁡(0,σθ2),\sqrt{NT}\,(\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0})\;\xrightarrow{d}\;N\!\left(0,\sigma_{\theta}^{2}\right),

where σθ2=κ0−2​Ω0\sigma_{\theta}^{2}=\kappa_{0}^{-2}\Omega_{0}, and κ0\kappa_{0} and Ω0\Omega_{0} are defined in Assumption 6(c).

Theorem 1 follows from the expansion

N​T​(θ^−θ0)=κ0−1​1N​T​∑i=1Nνi′​A0​εi+op​(1).\sqrt{NT}(\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0})=\kappa_{0}^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{NT}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nu_{i}^{\prime}A_{0}\varepsilon_{i}+o_{p}(1).

This expansion establishes first-order equivalence between FA-DML and an infeasible oracle estimator that knows the nuisance functions and factor spaces. Under the stated rate conditions, Neyman orthogonality and cross-fitting make the nuisance-estimation remainders negligible. Under the same conditions, double projection and separate training folds do the same for the factor-estimation remainders.

The resulting CLT permits valid inference without analytical bias correction. This contrasts with the interactive-effects least-squares framework of Bai, (2009), where heteroskedasticity and serial correlation can yield asymptotic bias.

Theorem 2 (Consistency of the variance estimator).

Under the conditions of Theorem 1, if Assumption 3(b) and Assumption 5(c) also hold,

σ^θ2→𝑝σθ2,\hat{\sigma}_{\theta}^{2}\xrightarrow{p}\sigma_{\theta}^{2},

where σθ2\sigma_{\theta}^{2} is defined in Theorem 1.

Theorem 2 complements Theorem 1 by showing that inference is fully feasible. The estimator σ^θ2\hat{\sigma}_{\theta}^{2} uses estimated nuisance functions and estimated factor spaces. Consistency of this plug-in estimator follows from the orthogonalization argument, together with the loading-weighted squared-error bounds in Assumption 3(b) and the fourth-moment condition in Assumption 5(c). In particular, the foldwise quadratic forms used in σ^θ2\hat{\sigma}_{\theta}^{2} are asymptotically equivalent to their infeasible counterparts based on νi\nu_{i}, εi\varepsilon_{i}, and A0A_{0}. Hence the numerator consistently estimates Ω0\Omega_{0}, while the denominator consistently estimates κ0\kappa_{0}. Together, Theorems 1 and 2 justify confidence intervals of the form

θ^±z1−α/2​σ^θN​T,\hat{\theta}\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\theta}}{\sqrt{NT}},

where z1−α/2z_{1-\alpha/2} is the (1−α/2)(1-\alpha/2)-quantile of the standard normal distribution.

4.4 Rank Selection

Theorems 1 and 2 treat rDr_{D} and rYr_{Y} as known. We estimate these dimensions using an alternating procedure that combines first-stage learning with nuclear-norm penalization. The complete procedure appears in Algorithm 2 in Appendix B. Here we define its terminal outputs and establish rank consistency and the validity of subsequent inference.

Let DD and YY denote the N×TN\times T matrices whose ii-th rows are Di′D_{i}^{\prime} and Yi′Y_{i}^{\prime}, respectively, and write X=(X1,…,XN)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{N}). For any vector-valued learner hh, let h⁡(X)h(X) denote the N×TN\times T matrix whose ii-th row is h​(Xi)′h(X_{i})^{\prime}. The primitive decompositions used for rank selection are

D=g0(X)+ΘD+V,ΘD=CDGD0′,D=g_{0}(X)+\Theta_{D}+V,\qquad\Theta_{D}=C_{D}G_{D}^{0\prime},

and

Y=m0(X)+ΘY+Ξ,ΘY=CG0′,Y=m_{0}(X)+\Theta_{Y}+\Xi,\qquad\Theta_{Y}=CG^{0\prime},

where the ii-th rows of CDC_{D}, CC, VV, and Ξ\Xi are CD,i′C_{D,i}^{\prime}, Ci′C_{i}^{\prime}, νi′\nu_{i}^{\prime}, and ξi′\xi_{i}^{\prime}, respectively.

Let g^(n​n)\hat{g}^{(nn)} and m^(n​n)\hat{m}^{(nn)} denote the terminal treatment and reduced-form learners used by the rank selector; Appendix B gives their complete construction. Define the effective residual perturbations

V~D=V−{g^(n​n)​(X)−g0​(X)},\widetilde{V}_{D}=V-\{\hat{g}^{(nn)}(X)-g_{0}(X)\},

and

Ξ~Y=Ξ−{m^(n​n)​(X)−m0​(X)}.\widetilde{\Xi}_{Y}=\Xi-\{\hat{m}^{(nn)}(X)-m_{0}(X)\}.

For positive tuning sequences ρD,ρY\rho_{D},\rho_{Y}, define the terminal low-rank estimates by

Θ^D=arg​minΘ∈ℝN×T​{12​‖D−g^(n​n)​(X)−Θ‖F2+ρD​‖Θ‖∗}.\hat{\Theta}_{D}=\mathrm{arg\,min}_{\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times T}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\|D-\hat{g}^{(nn)}(X)-\Theta\|_{F}^{2}+\rho_{D}\|\Theta\|_{*}\right\}.

Define Θ^Y\hat{\Theta}_{Y} by the same criterion using YY, m^(n​n)\hat{m}^{(nn)}, and ρY\rho_{Y}. For a fixed μ∈(−1/2,1/2)\mu\in(-1/2,1/2) and e∈{D,Y}e\in\{D,Y\}, define

r^e={0,s1​(Θ^e)=0,∑j=1min⁡{N,T}𝟏{sj(Θ^e)>ρe1/2−μs1(Θ^e)1/2+μ},s1​(Θ^e)>0.\hat{r}_{e}=\begin{cases}0,&s_{1}(\hat{\Theta}_{e})=0,\\[5.69054pt] \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\min\{N,T\}}\mathbf{1}\left\{s_{j}(\hat{\Theta}_{e})>\rho_{e}^{1/2-\mu}s_{1}(\hat{\Theta}_{e})^{1/2+\mu}\right\},&s_{1}(\hat{\Theta}_{e})>0.\end{cases}

Once the ranks are selected, Algorithm 1 continues to use the projected first-stage targets and double-projection score from Section 3.

Assumption 7 (Low-rank signal and final residual order).
  1. (a)

    For each e∈{D,Y}e\in\{D,Y\}, there exist constants 0<ce<Ce<∞0<c_{e}<C_{e}<\infty such that

    P(rank(Θe)=re,ceN​T≤sre(Θe)≤s1(Θe)≤CeN​T)→1.P\!\left(\operatorname{rank}(\Theta_{e})=r_{e},\quad c_{e}\sqrt{NT}\leq s_{r_{e}}(\Theta_{e})\leq s_{1}(\Theta_{e})\leq C_{e}\sqrt{NT}\right)\to 1.
  2. (b)

    The positive, possibly random tuning sequences ρD\rho_{D} and ρY\rho_{Y} satisfy

    ‖V~D‖opρD=Op​(1),‖Ξ~Y‖opρY=Op​(1),\frac{\|\widetilde{V}_{D}\|_{\operatorname{op}}}{\rho_{D}}=O_{p}(1),\qquad\frac{\|\widetilde{\Xi}_{Y}\|_{\operatorname{op}}}{\rho_{Y}}=O_{p}(1),

    and

    ρD=op​(N​T),ρY=op​(N​T).\rho_{D}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}),\qquad\rho_{Y}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}).

Assumption 7(a) imposes the signal separation used only for rank selection. It follows, for example, if the minimum and maximum eigenvalues of N−1​CD′​CDN^{-1}C_{D}^{\prime}C_{D}, N−1​C′​CN^{-1}C^{\prime}C, T−1GD0′GD0T^{-1}G_{D}^{0\prime}G_{D}^{0}, and T−1G0′G0T^{-1}G^{0\prime}G^{0} are bounded away from zero and infinity with probability approaching one. Those primitive Gram conditions are sufficient, not separately required by the rank theorem. Part (b) requires the effective residual perturbation to be no larger in stochastic order than ρD\rho_{D} or ρY\rho_{Y}, while these sequences remain asymptotically smaller than the N​T\sqrt{NT}-order signal. Unlike a hard domination inequality, this is a simple sufficient separation condition for the proof. It also rules out a final learner that absorbs a leading low-rank component. Its relation to first-stage prediction rates is discussed in Appendix D.

Theorem 3 (Consistency of rank selection).

Suppose Assumption 4(a) and Assumption 7 hold. Then, for any fixed μ∈(−1/2,1/2)\mu\in(-1/2,1/2),

P⁡(r^D=rD)→1,andP⁡(r^Y=rY)→1.P(\hat{r}_{D}=r_{D})\to 1,\quad\text{and}\quad P(\hat{r}_{Y}=r_{Y})\to 1.

Theorem 3 formalizes the singular-value separation behind the rank selector. For the treatment equation, the final residual matrix satisfies

D−g^(n​n)​(X)=ΘD+V~D.D-\hat{g}^{(nn)}(X)=\Theta_{D}+\widetilde{V}_{D}.

Assumption 7 implies ‖V~D‖op=op​(N​T)\|\widetilde{V}_{D}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}), while the nonzero singular values of ΘD\Theta_{D} are of order N​T\sqrt{NT}. If the residual perturbation is Op​(ρD)O_{p}(\rho_{D}) and ρD=op​(N​T)\rho_{D}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}), the nuclear-norm step estimates ΘD\Theta_{D} with operator-norm error of order ρD\rho_{D}. Hence the estimated singular values corresponding to the true factors remain of order N​T\sqrt{NT}, whereas the remaining singular values are of order at most ρD\rho_{D}. The threshold ρD1/2−μ​s1​(Θ^D)1/2+μ\rho_{D}^{1/2-\mu}s_{1}(\hat{\Theta}_{D})^{1/2+\mu} lies between these two orders, yielding P⁡(r^D=rD)→1P(\hat{r}_{D}=r_{D})\to 1. The same argument applies to the outcome equation.

This argument parallels the singular-value separation logic used in nuclear-norm penalized low-rank estimation and factor-number selection (Koltchinskii et al.,, 2011; Bai and Ng,, 2002; Ahn and Horenstein,, 2013, e.g.,). Here the residual matrices also contain errors from the estimated nuisance functions. The terminal residual bounds ensure that these errors preserve the separation needed for rank recovery.

Let θ^r^\widehat{\theta}_{\widehat{r}} and σ^θ,r^2\widehat{\sigma}_{\theta,\widehat{r}}^{2} be obtained by Algorithm 1 with (rD,rY)(r_{D},r_{Y}) replaced by the rank estimators (r^D,r^Y)(\hat{r}_{D},\hat{r}_{Y}) from Algorithm 2. Use a fixed measurable convention for SVD and eigenspace ties; when a selected rank is zero, take its projection to be zero and its residual-maker to be ITI_{T}. If a selected rank exceeds a corresponding training-fold matrix dimension, or if J^l=0\widehat{J}_{l}=0 for any split, set θ^r^=0\widehat{\theta}_{\widehat{r}}=0 and σ^θ,r^2=0\widehat{\sigma}_{\theta,\widehat{r}}^{2}=0. Under the assumptions below, this fallback occurs with probability tending to zero.

Corollary 1 (Inference with estimated ranks).

Under the assumptions of Theorems 1–3,

N​T​(θ^r^−θ0)→𝑑N⁡(0,σθ2),andσ^θ,r^2→𝑝σθ2,\sqrt{NT}\,(\widehat{\theta}_{\widehat{r}}-\theta_{0})\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,\sigma_{\theta}^{2}),\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{\sigma}_{\theta,\widehat{r}}^{2}\ \xrightarrow{p}\ \sigma_{\theta}^{2},

where σθ2\sigma_{\theta}^{2} is defined in Theorem 1.

Corollary 1 shows that preliminary rank selection does not affect first-order inference when the ranks are selected consistently. On the correct-rank event, the estimated-rank procedure coincides with the oracle-rank procedure. Because this event has probability approaching one, the limiting distribution and variance consistency carry over to the estimated-rank procedure.

5 Simulation Study

We use Monte Carlo experiments to assess coverage of FA-DML with known and data-selected factor dimensions. We compare FA-DML with a two-fold variant, standard DML without factor augmentation, and an OLS first-stage benchmark. These comparisons examine the finite-sample roles of sample separation, factor adjustment, and regularization. We also report the rank-selection frequencies.

5.1 Simulation Design and Implementation

We consider panels with (N,T)∈{100,200}×{50,100,200,300}(N,T)\in\{100,200\}\times\{50,100,200,300\}. The DGP follows the model in Section 2.1 and takes the form

Yi=Di​θ0+f0​(Xi)+GY0​CY,i∗+εi,Di=g0​(Xi)+GD0​CD,i+νi,Y_{i}=D_{i}\theta_{0}+f_{0}(X_{i})+G_{Y}^{0}C_{Y,i}^{*}+\varepsilon_{i},\qquad D_{i}=g_{0}(X_{i})+G_{D}^{0}C_{D,i}+\nu_{i},

where θ0=0.5\theta_{0}=0.5, Xi∈ℝT×pX_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times p}, and p=30p=30. Let Σd\Sigma_{d} denote the Toeplitz covariance matrix of dimension dd, with (s,t)(s,t) entry 0.5|s−t|0.5^{|s-t|}, and let β=(1,0.5,…,0.5p−1)′\beta=(1,0.5,\ldots,0.5^{p-1})^{\prime}. We consider linear nuisance functions, f0​(Xi)=g0​(Xi)=Xi​βf_{0}(X_{i})=g_{0}(X_{i})=X_{i}\beta, and quadratic nuisance functions, f0​(Xi)=g0​(Xi)=Xi​β+(Xi∘Xi)​βf_{0}(X_{i})=g_{0}(X_{i})=X_{i}\beta+(X_{i}\circ X_{i})\beta, where ∘\circ is the Hadamard product.

We let the treatment and structural outcome factor spaces share two of their three directions. Specifically, we set

GD0=[Gc​Gd],GY0=[Gc​Gy],G_{D}^{0}=\big[\,G^{c}\;\;G^{d}\,\big],\qquad G_{Y}^{0}=\big[\,G^{c}\;\;G^{y}\,\big],

where Gc∈ℝT×2G^{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 2} is common and Gd,Gy∈ℝTG^{d},G^{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{T} are equation-specific. In this baseline design with θ0=0.5\theta_{0}=0.5, rD=rY∗=3r_{D}=r_{Y}^{*}=3, while the reduced-form factor space is spanned by G0=[Gc,Gy,Gd]G^{0}=[G^{c},G^{y},G^{d}], with rY=4r_{Y}=4. We draw G0=ΣT1/2​G~​Σ41/2G^{0}=\Sigma_{T}^{1/2}\widetilde{G}\Sigma_{4}^{1/2}, where G~\widetilde{G} has i.i.d. N⁡(0,0.752)N(0,0.75^{2}) entries.

We write CD,i=(ΛD,ic′,BD,i)′C_{D,i}=({\Lambda_{D,i}^{c}}^{\prime},B_{D,i})^{\prime} and CY,i∗=(ΛY,ic′,BY,i)′C_{Y,i}^{*}=({\Lambda_{Y,i}^{c}}^{\prime},B_{Y,i})^{\prime}. We stack the loadings by unit and draw

ΛYc=ΣN1/2​Λ~Yc,ΛDc=ΛYc+ΣN1/2​Λ~Dc,BY=ΣN1/2​B~Y,BD=ΣN1/2​B~D,\Lambda_{Y}^{c}=\Sigma_{N}^{1/2}\,\tilde{\Lambda}_{Y}^{c},\qquad\Lambda_{D}^{c}=\Lambda_{Y}^{c}+\Sigma_{N}^{1/2}\,\tilde{\Lambda}_{D}^{c},\qquad B_{Y}=\Sigma_{N}^{1/2}\,\tilde{B}_{Y},\qquad B_{D}=\Sigma_{N}^{1/2}\,\tilde{B}_{D},

where Λ~Yc\widetilde{\Lambda}_{Y}^{c} has i.i.d. N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) entries, B~Y,B~D\widetilde{B}_{Y},\widetilde{B}_{D} have i.i.d. N⁡(0,2)N(0,2) entries, and Λ~Dc\widetilde{\Lambda}_{D}^{c} has i.i.d. N⁡(0,0.25)N(0,0.25) entries. These arrays are mutually independent and independent of G0G^{0}. Sharing ΛYc\Lambda_{Y}^{c} in ΛDc\Lambda_{D}^{c} induces treatment–outcome confounding along the common factor directions.

The kk-th covariate path, Xi​k∈ℝTX_{ik}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}, combines the two shared factor directions and an idiosyncratic Gaussian component according to

Xi​k=12∑q=120.5k−1Gcq+ΣT1/2Ux,i​k,k=1,…,p,X_{ik}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{q=1}^{2}0.5^{\,k-1}\,G^{c}_{q}+\Sigma_{T}^{1/2}\,U_{x,ik},\qquad k=1,\dots,p,

where GqcG^{c}_{q} is the qq-th column of GcG^{c}, and the Ux,i​kU_{x,ik} have i.i.d. N⁡(0,0.75)N(0,0.75) entries and are independent of the factors and loadings. This makes XiX_{i} correlated with both factor spaces but leaves a shared interactive component after covariate residualization.

Finally, the disturbances are conditionally heteroskedastic across units,

εi=σε,i​ε~i,νi=σν,i​ΣT1/2​ν~i,\varepsilon_{i}=\sigma_{\varepsilon,i}\,\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i},\qquad\nu_{i}=\sigma_{\nu,i}\,\Sigma_{T}^{1/2}\,\tilde{\nu}_{i},

where σε,i2,σν,i2​∼i.i.d.​Unif​[0.5,2]\sigma_{\varepsilon,i}^{2},\sigma_{\nu,i}^{2}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Unif}[0.5,2] are drawn once for each (N,T)(N,T) design and held fixed across Monte Carlo replications. The entries of ε~i\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{i} are i.i.d. N⁡(0,1)N(0,1), whereas those of ν~i\widetilde{\nu}_{i} are i.i.d. N⁡(0,0.75)N(0,0.75). These variables are independent across units and of all other primitives. Thus νi\nu_{i} is serially correlated, whereas εi\varepsilon_{i} is not. Cross-sectional dependence operates through the common factors and ΣN\Sigma_{N}-correlated loadings.

All first stages use the same additive cubic dictionary containing the first, second, and third powers of each covariate, without cross-products. Its dimension is p~=90\widetilde{p}=90. Both nuisance specifications lie in the span of this dictionary before factor projection. The quadratic design therefore introduces nonlinearity without dictionary approximation error. Each regularized specification is implemented with both Lasso and Elastic Net. OLS provides an unregularized first-stage benchmark.

For both Lasso and Elastic Net, we select the penalty coefficient separately at each regularized regression update using three-fold cross-validation within the relevant training sample. For Elastic Net, we fix the mixing parameter at ω=1/2\omega=1/2. Appendix E provides additional details of the simulation setting.

We implement three-fold FA-DML using Algorithm 1 with either known or selected ranks. Complete unit histories are randomly partitioned into three folds of sizes differing by at most one. Estimates are averaged over all six assignments of the treatment-training, outcome-training, and score-evaluation roles. The known-rank implementation uses (rD,rY)=(3,4)(r_{D},r_{Y})=(3,4) but still estimates the factor spaces and nuisance functions. In the selected-rank implementation, the iterative nuclear-norm procedure selects the two ranks on the full sample once per replication. These ranks are then held fixed across the six fold-role assignments.

To examine the role of sample splitting, we also consider a known-rank two-fold variant. Units are split into two equal folds. Both nuisance functions and factor spaces are estimated on one fold, and the double-projection score is evaluated on the other. The estimates are averaged after exchanging the fold roles. Relative to known-rank three-fold FA-DML, this changes both training-sample separation and size, so the comparison does not isolate separation at equal training-sample sizes. Standard DML uses the same two-fold arrangement but omits factor estimation and sets A^=IT\widehat{A}=I_{T}. This comparison holds the splitting scheme fixed.

To examine first-stage regularization, the OLS first-stage benchmark replaces both regularized nuisance fits with OLS using the same cubic dictionary. It retains the true ranks, factor augmentation, double-projection score, and three-fold cross-fitting of known-rank FA-DML. Additional implementation details are given in Appendix E.

5.2 Inference Results

Figure 1 compares the studentized statistic z=N​T​(θ^−θ0)/σ^θz=\sqrt{NT}(\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0})/\hat{\sigma}_{\theta} in the design with (N,T)=(100,100)(N,T)=(100,100). The comparison includes known-rank and selected-rank three-fold FA-DML, the known-rank two-fold variant, standard DML, and the OLS first-stage benchmark. The first four methods use Lasso, and all five are evaluated on the same simulated panels within each nuisance design. All distributions use the same horizontal and density scales. Figure 2 in Appendix E adds the Elastic Net implementations.

For known-rank FA-DML, the studentized distribution is close to the standard normal benchmark, with a modest rightward shift under linear nuisance functions and a mean close to zero under quadratic nuisance functions. The selected-rank distribution nearly overlaps it in both panels. At this sample size the selected pair is correct in 98.4%98.4\% of linear and 98.5%98.5\% of quadratic replications.

The distribution for the two-fold variant is shifted to the right. This pattern is consistent with the same-training-fold interaction discussed in Section 3.2, although the comparison does not identify that interaction separately from the change in training-sample sizes. The distribution for standard DML is displaced far to the right in this design, which retains interactive confounding after covariate adjustment. For the OLS first-stage benchmark, the studentized statistic is shifted to the left of zero and is less dispersed than the standard normal under both nuisance specifications. The benchmark’s undercoverage at this sample size is thus accompanied by a leftward displacement of the studentized statistic. The complete figure in the appendix shows similar qualitative patterns with Elastic Net.

Table 1 reports coverage of nominal 95%95\% confidence intervals across the sample-size grid. Coverage for known-rank and selected-rank FA-DML ranges from 93.4%93.4\% to 95.9%95.9\% in the linear design and from 92.6%92.6\% to 95.8%95.8\% in the quadratic design. Undercoverage in the quadratic design is concentrated in shorter panels, particularly with Elastic Net. Selected-rank coverage differs from known-rank coverage by at most 0.70.7 percentage points. At (N,T)=(100,100)(N,T)=(100,100), the corresponding Lasso coverages are 94.0%94.0\% and 93.9%93.9\% in the linear design and 95.3%95.3\% and 95.2%95.2\% in the quadratic design.

The two-fold variant undercovers substantially. Its coverage improves with NN at each fixed TT and generally declines as TT increases at fixed NN. Standard DML has zero empirical coverage throughout the reported grid. OLS coverage increases with TT, but undercoverage in shorter panels can give way to overcoverage: at N=100N=100, coverage rises from 65.8%65.8\% to 99.4%99.4\% in the linear design and from 63.2%63.2\% to 99.5%99.5\% in the quadratic design as TT increases from 5050 to 300300. Across this baseline grid, regularized three-fold FA-DML is closer to nominal coverage than the benchmark methods.

5.3 Rank-Selection Performance

We evaluate the rank selector using the same DGP and sample-size grid. Table 2 reports the marginal frequencies of correctly selecting rD=3r_{D}=3 and rY=4r_{Y}=4. Each rank is recovered in at least 95.0%95.0\% of replications in every design, in at least 98.4%98.4\% when T≥100T\geq 100, and in all replications when T≥200T\geq 200. Performance is similar across Lasso and Elastic Net and across the two nuisance specifications.

6 Minimum Wages and Lower-Tail Wage Inequality

We study whether the negative relationship between minimum wages and lower-tail wage inequality persists after flexible adjustment for observed workforce composition and latent interactive heterogeneity. States may respond differently to common economic shocks, and these responses may be related to both minimum-wage policy and wage inequality. FA-DML accommodates this heterogeneity beyond additive state and year effects. Appendix F.2 presents an additional application to branching deregulation and income inequality.

Autor et al., (2016) find that minimum wages compress the lower tail of the U.S. wage distribution. We revisit this relationship using a panel of all 5050 states from 19791979 to 20122012, with 1,7001{,}700 state-year observations. We use their state-level wage percentiles and minimum wages, constructed from the Current Population Survey Merged Outgoing Rotation Groups. Our outcome is

Yi​t=log⁡wi​t​(50)−log⁡wi​t​(10),Y_{it}=\log w_{it}(50)-\log w_{it}(10),

where wi​t​(q)w_{it}(q) is the qq-th percentile of wages in state ii and year tt. The treatment Di​tD_{it} is the log real effective state minimum wage. Thus θ0\theta_{0} is the elasticity of the 50/10 wage ratio with respect to the real minimum wage.

Unlike Autor et al., (2016), we do not measure the treatment as the minimum wage’s “bite” relative to the state median. Because their outcome is also expressed relative to the median, sampling error in the median enters both sides of the regression, a division-bias problem (Borjas,, 1980) that they address with instrumental variables. Using the minimum-wage level avoids this shared component, so our linear specification targets a different parameter from their nonlinear specification in the bite.

The original control dictionary contains four state-year characteristics: mean age, female employment share, non-white employment share, and the log sum of the hours-adjusted CPS earnings weights. The expanded dictionary contains 3232 features obtained from a degree-four polynomial expansion after collinear terms are removed. These controls allow observed composition to affect wages flexibly. Interactive effects allow common shocks, such as business-cycle fluctuations, to affect states differently. Such heterogeneity may be correlated with both minimum-wage policy and wage inequality and is not absorbed by additive state and year effects.

We estimate the first stages by Lasso and by random forests with each dictionary. The Lasso penalty is a multiple of log⁡p/(N​T)\sqrt{\log p/(NT)}, with the multiplier chosen from [0.01,10][0.01,10] by three-fold cross-validation. The random forest uses 500500 trees of maximum depth three, a minimum leaf size of 3030, and p\sqrt{p} candidate features per split. FA-DML follows Algorithm 1, repeated over 1515 random sample splits and aggregated with the median adjustment of Chernozhukov et al., (2018, Section 3.4).

The benchmarks are pooled OLS, two-way fixed effects (TWFE), standard DML, and the interactive fixed-effects estimator of Bai, (2009) (OLS-IFE). Standard DML uses two-fold cross-fitting over states and cross-validated Lasso on standardized controls. OLS-IFE uses the iterative estimator of Bai, (2009) with non-clustered standard errors. For OLS-IFE, rr counts structural outcome factors. The FA-DML outcome rank instead refers to the reduced-form factor space. Their rank grids are therefore not directly comparable.

Applying Algorithm 2 with Lasso to the original dictionary, with the calibration in Appendix F.1, selects (r^D,r^Y)=(2,3)(\hat{r}_{D},\hat{r}_{Y})=(2,3). We use this pair as the primary specification for both dictionaries and learners and treat other dimensions as sensitivity checks. Table 3 reports the results.

At the selected ranks, the Lasso and random-forest estimates are −0.1103-0.1103 and −0.1167-0.1167 with the original controls and −0.1088-0.1088 and −0.1120-0.1120 with the expanded controls. All four 95%95\% intervals exclude zero. A 10%10\% increase in the real minimum wage is thus associated with a roughly 1.1%1.1\% lower 50/10 wage ratio, and this estimate is stable across dictionaries and learners.

The benchmark estimates respond differently to the control dictionary. Expanding the controls changes pooled OLS from −0.0213-0.0213 to −0.1327-0.1327 and TWFE from −0.0249-0.0249 to −0.0647-0.0647; their intervals include zero with the original controls but exclude it with the expanded dictionary. Standard DML estimates remain close to zero and imprecise under both dictionaries. OLS-IFE point estimates remain negative and decrease in magnitude as rr increases. Their confidence intervals exclude zero at all ranks considered with the original controls. With the expanded controls, they exclude zero for r=2,…,5r=2,\ldots,5 but include zero at r=6r=6.

For FA-DML, this finding also extends beyond the selected rank pair (2,3)(2,3). The 2020 equal-rank specifications with rD=rY=r∈{2,…,6}r_{D}=r_{Y}=r\in\{2,\ldots,6\} yield estimates between −0.1652-0.1652 and −0.1152-0.1152. Across the full grid in Appendix F.1, all 6060 estimates lie between −0.1652-0.1652 and −0.1003-0.1003, and every reported interval excludes zero. Results are similar across learners: for each rank pair and control dictionary, the Lasso and random-forest estimates differ by at most 0.01160.0116.

Overall, the results indicate that higher minimum wages are associated with lower wage inequality at the bottom of the distribution, even after flexible adjustment for observed workforce composition and latent interactive heterogeneity.

7 Conclusion

Learning latent factor spaces from panel residuals introduces estimation errors that standard DML orthogonality does not automatically control. FA-DML addresses these errors through double projection and separate training folds for the treatment and reduced-form equations. Double projection makes the factor–factor interaction a product of errors from the two estimated spaces. Separate training folds remove same-unit pairings in their leading disturbance components. Under the stated conditions, the estimator delivers oracle-equivalent inference without analytical bias correction. We also develop a consistent rank selector and show that estimating the factor dimensions preserves inference results.

A natural extension is to dynamic panels with predetermined regressors. Such an extension would require adapting the score and sample-splitting scheme to account for dependence between current disturbances and future covariates. Extending the analysis to weak factors is another direction for future work.

Appendix B Data-Driven Rank-Selection Procedure

Section 4.4 defines the terminal rank estimators used in the theoretical results. This appendix provides the complete alternating procedure that constructs their terminal learners and low-rank estimates. The selector uses nuclear-norm penalization, a standard convex relaxation of rank regularization used in low-rank matrix estimation and matrix completion (Candès and Recht,, 2009; Recht et al.,, 2010; Mazumder et al.,, 2010; Koltchinskii et al.,, 2011), including in econometric panel settings (Athey et al.,, 2021; Chernozhukov et al.,, 2026; Moon and Weidner,, 2026).

For M∈ℝN×TM\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times T}, let q=min⁡{N,T}q=\min\{N,T\} and write its singular value decomposition as

M=U​diag⁡(s1,…,sq)​V′,s1≥⋯≥sq≥0.M=U\operatorname{diag}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{q})V^{\prime},\qquad s_{1}\geq\cdots\geq s_{q}\geq 0.

For ζ>0\zeta>0, define the singular-value thresholding operator

SVT⁡(M,ζ)=U​diag⁡{(s1−ζ)+,…,(sq−ζ)+}​V′,\mathrm{SVT}(M,\zeta)=U\operatorname{diag}\{(s_{1}-\zeta)_{+},\ldots,(s_{q}-\zeta)_{+}\}V^{\prime},

where (a)+=max⁡{a,0}(a)_{+}=\max\{a,0\}.

Let DD and YY denote the N×TN\times T matrices whose ii-th rows are Di′D_{i}^{\prime} and Yi′Y_{i}^{\prime}, respectively, and write X=(X1,…,XN)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{N}). For any vector-valued learner hh, let h⁡(X)h(X) denote the N×TN\times T matrix whose ii-th row is h​(Xi)′h(X_{i})^{\prime}.

Proof of Theorem 3

Proof.

We prove the result for the treatment equation. At the final nuclear-norm step, the matrix supplied to singular-value thresholding is

D−g^(n​n)​(X)=ΘD+V~D.D-\widehat{g}^{(nn)}(X)=\Theta_{D}+\widetilde{V}_{D}.

Because the terminal objective defining Θ^D\widehat{\Theta}_{D} in Section 4.4 is the proximal problem for the nuclear norm,

sj(Θ^D)={sj(ΘD+V~D)−ρD}+,j=1,…,min{N,T}.s_{j}(\widehat{\Theta}_{D})=\{s_{j}(\Theta_{D}+\widetilde{V}_{D})-\rho_{D}\}_{+},\qquad j=1,\ldots,\min\{N,T\}.

Assumption 7(a) implies that, with probability approaching one, there are constants 0<cD<CD<∞0<c_{D}<C_{D}<\infty such that

cDN​T≤srD(ΘD)≤s1(ΘD)≤CDN​T,sj(ΘD)=0(j>rD).c_{D}\sqrt{NT}\leq s_{r_{D}}(\Theta_{D})\leq s_{1}(\Theta_{D})\leq C_{D}\sqrt{NT},\qquad s_{j}(\Theta_{D})=0\quad(j>r_{D}).

For j>rDj>r_{D}, Weyl’s inequality and the soft-thresholding formula give

sj​(Θ^D)≤{‖V~D‖op−ρD}+≤‖V~D‖op=Op​(ρD).s_{j}(\widehat{\Theta}_{D})\leq\{\|\widetilde{V}_{D}\|_{\operatorname{op}}-\rho_{D}\}_{+}\leq\|\widetilde{V}_{D}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=O_{p}(\rho_{D}).

For j≤rDj\leq r_{D}, the same inequality gives

Appendix D Discussion of the First-Stage Rates

Assumption 2 bounds the total conditional prediction errors of the feasible first-stage procedures relative to g0∗g_{0}^{*} and m0∗m_{0}^{*}, including the effects of estimated factor projections. Proposition 1 transfers these rates to the evaluation fold and controls the nuisance-error remainder R1​iR_{1i}. Assumption 3 specifies loading-weighted conditions for the training-fold factor expansions and the evaluation-fold factor–nuisance interactions. Accordingly, r¯g\bar{r}_{g} and r¯m\bar{r}_{m} describe ordinary prediction errors, while ηg\eta_{g} and ηm\eta_{m} describe the corresponding loading-weighted quantities.

Lasso rate illustration.

Consider a projected-Lasso implementation with a dictionary Zi=Z⁡(Xi)∈ℝT×pZ_{i}=Z(X_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times p}, where p=pN​T≥2p=p_{NT}\geq 2 is the number of dictionary features. Suppose that g0g_{0} and m0m_{0} admit approximately sparse representations

g0​(Xi)=Zi​βg0+rg​(Xi),m0​(Xi)=Zi​βm0+rm​(Xi),g_{0}(X_{i})=Z_{i}\beta_{g}^{0}+r_{g}(X_{i}),\qquad m_{0}(X_{i})=Z_{i}\beta_{m}^{0}+r_{m}(X_{i}),

where βg0,βm0∈ℝp\beta_{g}^{0},\beta_{m}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} have at most sgs_{g} and sms_{m} nonzero coordinates, respectively. The TT-vector maps rgr_{g} and rmr_{m} are the approximation errors. Let bg,N​Tb_{g,NT} and bm,N​Tb_{m,NT} be nonnegative deterministic bounds on their normalized conditional approximation norms ‖rg‖P,2\|r_{g}\|_{P,2} and ‖rm‖P,2\|r_{m}\|_{P,2}.

Suppose the complete feasible Lasso procedure satisfies Assumption 2(a)–(b) with vanishing deterministic rates such that

r¯g≲sg​log⁡pN​T+bg,N​T,r¯m≲sm​log⁡pN​T+bm,N​T.\bar{r}_{g}\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{s_{g}\log p}{NT}}+b_{g,NT},\qquad\bar{r}_{m}\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{s_{m}\log p}{NT}}+b_{m,NT}.

Since n3≍Nn_{3}\asymp N, substituting these bounds into Assumption 2(c) gives the sufficient product-rate restriction

N​T​(sg​log⁡pN​T+bg,N​T)\displaystyle\sqrt{NT}\left(\sqrt{\frac{s_{g}\log p}{NT}}+b_{g,NT}\right)
×(sm​log⁡pN​T+bm,N​T+sg​log⁡pN​T+bg,N​T)=o⁡(1).\displaystyle\times\left(\sqrt{\frac{s_{m}\log p}{NT}}+b_{m,NT}+\sqrt{\frac{s_{g}\log p}{NT}}+b_{g,NT}\right)=o(1).

In the exactly sparse case, rg=rm=0r_{g}=r_{m}=0, so the approximation bounds can be taken as bg,N​T=bm,N​T=0b_{g,NT}=b_{m,NT}=0. The sufficient restriction for part (c) then simplifies to

(sg​sm+sg)​log⁡p=o⁡(N​T).\bigl(\sqrt{s_{g}s_{m}}+s_{g}\bigr)\log p=o(\sqrt{NT}).

The prediction, loading-weighted, and residual conditions in Assumptions 2, 3, and 5(d) jointly restrict the complete feasible fitting procedure and the admissible growth of NN and TT.

Connection to rank selection.

For the terminal learners used by Algorithm 2, the rank-selection residual conditions concern prediction errors relative to the unprojected functions g0g_{0} and m0m_{0}. Recall that

V~D=V−{g^(n​n)​(X)−g0​(X)},Ξ~Y=Ξ−{m^(n​n)​(X)−m0​(X)}.\widetilde{V}_{D}=V-\{\hat{g}^{(nn)}(X)-g_{0}(X)\},\qquad\widetilde{\Xi}_{Y}=\Xi-\{\hat{m}^{(nn)}(X)-m_{0}(X)\}.

By the triangle inequality and ∥⋅∥op≤∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\|\cdot\|_{F},

‖V~D‖op≤‖V‖op+‖g^(n​n)​(X)−g0​(X)‖F,\|\widetilde{V}_{D}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\|V\|_{\operatorname{op}}+\|\hat{g}^{(nn)}(X)-g_{0}(X)\|_{F},

and

‖Ξ~Y‖op≤‖Ξ‖op+‖m^(n​n)​(X)−m0​(X)‖F.\|\widetilde{\Xi}_{Y}\|_{\operatorname{op}}\leq\|\Xi\|_{\operatorname{op}}+\|\hat{m}^{(nn)}(X)-m_{0}(X)\|_{F}.

The following conditions imply that both effective residuals are op​(N​T)o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}):

‖V‖op=op​(N​T),1N​T​‖g^(n​n)​(X)−g0​(X)‖F2=op​(1),\|V\|_{\operatorname{op}}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}),\qquad\frac{1}{NT}\|\hat{g}^{(nn)}(X)-g_{0}(X)\|_{F}^{2}=o_{p}(1),

and

‖Ξ‖op=op​(N​T),1N​T​‖m^(n​n)​(X)−m0​(X)‖F2=op​(1).\|\Xi\|_{\operatorname{op}}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}),\qquad\frac{1}{NT}\|\hat{m}^{(nn)}(X)-m_{0}(X)\|_{F}^{2}=o_{p}(1).

Thus

‖V~D‖op=op​(N​T),‖Ξ~Y‖op=op​(N​T).\|\widetilde{V}_{D}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}),\qquad\|\widetilde{\Xi}_{Y}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=o_{p}(\sqrt{NT}).

These conditions separate the effective residuals from the factor-signal scale. Assumption 7(b) further requires

‖V~D‖op=Op​(ρD),‖Ξ~Y‖op=Op​(ρY).\|\widetilde{V}_{D}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=O_{p}(\rho_{D}),\qquad\|\widetilde{\Xi}_{Y}\|_{\operatorname{op}}=O_{p}(\rho_{Y}).

The terminal fits and tuning sequences used by Algorithm 2 are required to satisfy these bounds jointly. These requirements concern the unprojected targets g0g_{0} and m0m_{0}, whereas Assumption 2 concerns the projected first-stage targets used for inference.

Appendix E Additional Simulation Details and Evidence

First-stage fitting.

For both Lasso and Elastic Net, the T×90T\times 90 series dictionary for unit ii contains the coordinatewise first, second, and third powers of the original covariates, without cross-products. At each factor-augmented update, the current time-series residual-maker is applied to both the TT-vector pseudo-outcome and every column of the dictionary. The projected arrays are then stacked over the relevant training units before the learner is refit. This implements the projected targets g0∗g_{0}^{*} and m0∗m_{0}^{*}.

For both Lasso and Elastic Net, we select the penalty coefficient by three-fold cross-validation over a common grid of 31 candidate values ranging from 10−3/N​T10^{-3}/\sqrt{NT} to 11. The Elastic Net mixing parameter is fixed at ω=1/2\omega=1/2.

Writing y~\widetilde{y} and Z~\widetilde{Z} for the stacked training response and dictionary, and ntrn_{\mathrm{tr}} for their number of rows, the regularized regression minimizes over b∈ℝp~b\in\mathbb{R}^{\widetilde{p}}

12​ntr​‖y~−Z~​b‖22+α⁡{ω​‖b‖1+1−ω2​‖b‖22},\frac{1}{2n_{\mathrm{tr}}}\|\widetilde{y}-\widetilde{Z}b\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha\left\{\omega\|b\|_{1}+\frac{1-\omega}{2}\|b\|_{2}^{2}\right\},

with ω=1\omega=1 for Lasso and ω=1/2\omega=1/2 for Elastic Net. The regressions have no additional intercept, and dictionary columns are not standardized. In factor-augmented regressions, the response and dictionary are projected as described above, whereas standard DML uses unprojected data. The OLS first-stage benchmark uses the same dictionary and factor-projection steps, replacing the regularized fit with unpenalized least squares. Fold-specific point estimates and variance estimates are averaged over the six role assignments for the three-fold specifications and over the two assignments for the two-fold specifications.

Rank selection.

In this simulation study, we select the treatment and reduced-form outcome ranks separately on the full sample, alternating nuclear-norm soft thresholding with penalized learner updates. When the selected pair equals the true pair (3,4)(3,4), selected-rank FA-DML reduces to known-rank FA-DML, and we use the known-rank estimates for that replication.

Additional distribution comparisons.

Figure 2 supplements Figure 1 by including the Elastic Net specifications. For specifications appearing in both figures, the histogram bins are identical. All distributions use common horizontal and density scales without smoothing.

Appendix F Additional Evidence for the Empirical Applications

This appendix reports factor-dimension sensitivity for the minimum-wage application and presents the branching-deregulation application. The sensitivity grid contains the 1515 pairs with 2≤rD≤rY≤62\leq r_{D}\leq r_{Y}\leq 6, for two learners and two control dictionaries. The inference results in Section 4 apply to the true or consistently selected ranks.

F.1 Minimum-Wage Estimates across Factor Dimensions

For the minimum-wage application, Algorithm 2 is applied to the original dictionary with cross-validated Lasso, ρD=ρY=0.25\rho_{D}=\rho_{Y}=0.25, and μ=0.001\mu=0.001, and it selects (2,3)(2,3). The penalty level differs from the simulation design because the nuclear-norm penalty scales with the residual matrices.

Table 5 extends the diagonal comparison in Table 3 to 2≤rD≤rY≤62\leq r_{D}\leq r_{Y}\leq 6. The data, control dictionaries, and first-stage settings are those of Section 6. All 6060 estimates are negative, ranging from −0.1652-0.1652 to −0.1003-0.1003, and every interval excludes zero. For a given pair and dictionary, the Lasso and random-forest estimates differ by at most 0.01160.0116. Magnitudes depend more on rDr_{D} than on rYr_{Y}.

F.2 Branching Deregulation and Income Inequality

Beck et al., (2010) find that intrastate branching deregulation reduced income inequality in a two-way fixed-effects specification. We ask whether this conclusion survives flexible adjustment for observed covariates and interactive state-time heterogeneity. As in the original study, the panel covers 4848 states and the District of Columbia from 19761976 to 20062006, excluding Delaware and South Dakota, for N×T=49×31=1,519N\times T=49\times 31=1{,}519 observations.

The outcome is the logit transformation of the Gini coefficient,

Yi​t=log{gi​t/(1−gi​t)},Di​t=𝟏{t>ti∗},Y_{it}=\log\{g_{it}/(1-g_{it})\},\qquad D_{it}=\mathbf{1}\{t>t_{i}^{*}\},

where gi​tg_{it} is the Gini coefficient and ti∗t_{i}^{*} is the year of intrastate branching deregulation, so the treatment equals one from the year after deregulation, as in Beck et al., (2010). The parameter θ0\theta_{0} is a common effect on the log-odds of the Gini coefficient, and the specification does not allow effects to vary by adoption cohort or event time. For the binary treatment, the treatment equation is the factor-augmented linear probability model of Section 2.

The original dictionary contains eight controls: growth in gross state product (GSP) per capita, the shares of Black residents, high-school dropouts, and female-headed households, the unemployment rate, log GSP per capita, log population, and population dispersion. A degree-four polynomial expansion, with nearly collinear terms removed, gives 302302 controls. Interactive effects allow common economic shocks to affect states differently. Identification rests on Assumption 1.

The benchmarks and the random-forest settings follow Section 6, and Lasso uses the self-normalized penalty of Belloni et al., (2012). FA-DML follows Algorithm 1 with the same 1515-split median adjustment. Algorithm 2 selects (rD,rY)=(2,3)(r_{D},r_{Y})=(2,3), which we use as the primary specification for both dictionaries and learners. Table 6 also reports FA-DML with rD=rY=r∈{2,…,6}r_{D}=r_{Y}=r\in\{2,\ldots,6\}.

With the original controls, pooled OLS, TWFE, and standard DML all give negative estimates with intervals excluding zero, and the TWFE estimate is −0.0289-0.0289. With the expanded dictionary, TWFE remains negative at −0.0208-0.0208, pooled OLS is close to zero, and standard DML is much less precise. The benchmark results therefore depend on both the estimator and the control set. The OLS-IFE intervals all include zero with the original dictionary, and only r=4r=4 yields an interval excluding zero with the expanded dictionary.

At the selected pair (2,3)(2,3), the Lasso and random-forest estimates are −0.0019-0.0019 and −0.0017-0.0017 with the original controls and −0.0023-0.0023 and −0.0015-0.0015 with the expanded controls, and all four intervals include zero. Over all 1515 pairs with 2≤rD≤rY≤62\leq r_{D}\leq r_{Y}\leq 6, the estimates range from −0.0069-0.0069 to 0.00660.0066, and every interval includes zero. With the self-normalized penalty, Lasso retains few controls, so its estimates are nearly identical across the two dictionaries. Once interactive heterogeneity is allowed, the estimated effect of deregulation is close to zero, so the TWFE estimate is sensitive to how latent confounding is modeled. The common-coefficient specification does not rule out cohort-specific or dynamic effects.
